en: Regarding the establishment of this title for the *Lianzhu ji* (A String of Pearls:
A Brief Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of Prajñā), it is intended to show that there is no reliance on personal opinion.

It means that the text of this commentary consists entirely of the "spiritual snakes" and "night-shining gems" of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, as well as the "red fields," "cinnabar wilds," and "vermilion depths."
The moon is that which was once full; it is merely strung together with red silk and golden thread to serve as a record, resembling the Pearl Mound at Cangwu.
This preface was composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Hui of Songyufeng, who is about to explain this commentary. The text has two parts:
first, the title, which has two sub-sections: [1.1] the main title and [1.2] the sub-title.
First, the title of the commentary is presented.
Now, there are two kinds of titles:

that which is placed at the beginning of a sutra is called the "sutra title," while that which is set before a commentary is called the "commentary title"; what follows here is the title of the commentary.
"Prajñā" and so forth refer to the sūtra that is to be explained, while "Brief Commentary" (Lüshù) refers to the commentary that is capable of explaining it.
By taking the title of the sūtra to be explained and the portion of the commentary that explains it, one forms a possessive compound (tatpuruṣa) based on another name;
if one says "the commentary [on it]," it is a dependent determinative compound (śeṣa-tatpuruṣa).
“Brief” (*lue*) refers to the abbreviation of essentials; it does not mean that there is a separate extensive commentary.
“Together with the preface” (*bing xu*) means that it includes a preface as well.

Regarding the second point, the manifestation of the honorary title of the translator: following the *Jiake jingshu* (Annotated Sutra Commentary) carved by Master Jin of Jingkou, the Patriarch himself inscribed upon it: “In the second year of Chang’an, while Fa-zang was at leisure from translating sutras at Qingchan Monastery in the capital, Zheng Gong of Yingyang—who served concurrently as Director of the Ministry of Rites and Acting Chief Administrator of Yongzhou—repeatedly and earnestly requested that he produce this brief commentary.”
The phrase "in the leisure time of translating scriptures" does not mean that he had previously participated in a translation assembly.
As for the term "śramaṇa," this is translated as "diligent in cessation.
The following two characters are the master of the commentary’s own given name.
"Narration" (shu) is a humble expression meaning "to narrate without composing.
Part Two: The Main Text, in three sections:
First, the general presentation of the title and its significance; Second, the opening of the chapters and the explanation of the text; Third, the celebration and dedication of merit.
The first part consists of two sections:
first, a general exposition of the profound framework to reveal the great significance of Prajñā, which has three sub-sections;
first, a direct exposition of its profound depth, which has three further sub-sections:
First, transcending words to point to the essence, in two parts:
first, the mystery of the essence.
Regarding the phrase "Now, as for... (*fú yǐ*) and so forth: *fú* is a particle used to introduce speech, while *yǐ* indicates the reason or cause.

"True Source" (zhényuán) means that which is not false or deluded thought is called "True," and the essential nature of all phenomena is called "Source"; it is precisely the signless True Suchness (tathatā) of the Prajñā of Real Mark.
The Qingliang Commentary on the Samādhi of the Limit of a Kṣaṇa states:

"To exhaustively investigate the true source of phenomena means that when one exhaustively investigates the temporal characteristics of a kṣaṇa and finds them all to be quiescent, then the kṣaṇa is without limit."
"Because one realizes that pure *tathatā* (suchness) is fundamentally without marks (*animitta*).
Thus, markless *tathatā* is taken as the true source.
Zhenyuan said:
"Delusively following the transformations of objects, its substance shifts with appearances; yet when struck, the True Source surges forth, vast and boundless.
He takes the secret treasury of the jewel in the robe to be the true source of the nature of things.
Cao Tang said:
"The mind of prajñā is the substance of all dharmas.
He also said:
"True emptiness is precisely the source of the numinous and wondrous mind.

This is because its fundamental nature is the single mind of True Suchness (tathatā); when this unites with birth-and-death, it is termed the *ālayavijñāna*, which transforms to give rise to the various phenomena of the sense organs, the physical body, the objective world, form, and so forth. When these are investigated, they are found to have no substantiality and return to the emptiness of the true mind. Thus, the emptiness of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is the fundamental source of all phenomena; therefore, it is called the 'true source.'"
The Treatise states: "Because the meaning of emptiness exists, all phenomena are established.
The Sūtra says: "From the root of non-abiding, all phenomena are established."
Zhenguang said:
"Non-abiding, the emptiness of nature, and suchness are all alternative names for the true mark.
The Master of the Commentary further said:
"To cause the capacity [of the practitioner] to realize the true source and enter the ocean of fruition" means that the ocean of fruition is taken as the true source.
"Suvān" (素範) signifies: "su" (素) represents being free from flaw, and "fàn" (範) maintains one's own nature.
This means that its substance is like ice and frost, and its nature is like pearls and jade; even when situated within the mire of afflictions (*kleśa*), it does not alter its firm whiteness.
The Treatise states: "Within the essence of suchness (*tathatā*), all defiled phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭadharma*) exceeding the number of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas are entirely empty, void, and non-existent."
The Master of the Commentary said:
"The fundamental model transcends conceptual thought; thus, both emptiness and existence are simultaneously extinguished.
As for "profound and vast": "profound" refers to deep mystery, and "vast" denotes expansive distance.
The Master of the Commentary further stated:
"Vast and boundless, it transcends sight and hearing; profound and infinite, it defies thought and deliberation.
The Treatise says: "Transcending the realm of contemplation and severing the domain of observation—how could this be captured by the means of a trap or a net?"
The "quan" (fish trap) is the device for catching fish;
the "jie" (rabbit snare) is the net for trapping rabbits.
These are used as metaphors for how discursive talk and conceptual thought are separated from ultimate truth.
Below "Wondrous Enlightenment" (Miaojue), the second is the wondrous function, which is the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*guanzhao*).
Zhenguó said:
"Because it is detached from both the subject that perceives and the object perceived, it is called Wondrous Enlightenment."
The Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata has now attained the wondrous, luminous awakening of emptiness.
The Śāstra says: "Because one awakens to the source of the mind, it is called ultimate awakening.
Furthermore, the Śāstra says: "The wisdom of *saj-jñāna* consists solely of awakened illumination; there is not a single dharma that is not awakening."
The Master of the Commentary then said:
"It is the wisdom that wondrously realizes the true source.
As for "profound path" (*xuanyou*), *you* means the Way (*dao*) and the cause (*yin*).
It is said that this wondrous awakening is the correct path for entering the true source and the profound cause for attaining the sublime fruit.
Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "By means of this wondrous wisdom, one overturns the faults of birth and death until reaching the limit of true emptiness."
"Profound and vast" means that the ocean of Prajñā is so deep it cannot be fathomed.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The great ocean of wisdom—only a Buddha can reach its bottom."
Regarding the phrase "transcending words and signs," the Sūtra states: "The meaning of Prajñā is nameless and unspeakable.
It further says: "True Prajñā is pure as space; it is without cognition or vision, without action or conditions."
An ancient worthy said:
"The essence is fundamentally beyond dependence; both name and description are quiescent; therefore, it transcends words and mental images.
The previous statement that the fish-trap and rabbit-snare are metaphors for words and images is cited alternately here merely to make the composition elegant.
The *Zhouyi lue li* states: "Words arise from images; therefore, one may seek out words to observe the images.
Images arise from intentions; therefore, one may seek out images to observe the intentions."
The mind is fully expressed through symbols, and symbols are made manifest through words; therefore, one grasps the meaning and forgets the symbol, and grasps the symbol and forgets the word.
It is just as a snare exists for the sake of the rabbit—once the rabbit is caught, one forgets the snare;
a fish-trap exists for the sake of the fish—once the fish is caught, one forgets the trap.
"One who clings to words does not grasp the images; one who clings to images does not grasp the meaning.
Thus, those who wish to study should abandon the expedient expressions (*vyavahāra*) to seek the ultimate intent (*artha*).
Yet, contemporary commentators claim that the principle of wondrous emptiness and true awakening is perfect while words are partial, and that its characteristics are ultimately ineffable.
Therefore, the Master of the Commentary said:
"The profound and mysterious Way is so vast that its limits are rarely found through names and words;
the boundless and pristine model is so expansive that its source cannot be exhausted even when its manifestations are observed."

This means that words are forgotten through words and signs are forgotten through signs; it does not mean that one must first purge all things, block the senses from sights and sounds, or achieve a state of silent vacuity before it can be considered the Truth.
Question: One speaks only when the time is right; to speak when it is not the proper time is called excessive speech.

Furthermore, the emergence of this teaching is intended to cause practitioners to generate the great resolve and cultivate extensive practices, thereby destroying external attachments, turning away from the small vehicle, severing obstacles to attain the fruit, and benefiting sentient beings.
By what means does the Master of the Commentary suddenly discuss the source of those ten thousand dharmas—the wondrous enlightenment of the ultimate fruit?
He replies:
It is because he wishes to reveal that the causes cultivated are identical to the enlightenment of the stage of fruition.

Mañjuśrī first inquired into the causes of the original arising, and the Supreme Sage first set forth the ultimate fruit; yet if one's nature were not that of gold or jade, though it be carved, it could not become a precious vessel.
Therefore, a sutra says: "If one cannot understand one's own mind, how can one know the right path?
Furthermore, it was asked:
"If you were merely recounting profound sudden-vehicle sutras such as the *Śūraṅgama* and the *Complete Enlightenment*, your lofty discourse would indeed be acceptable."
Now, it is clear that this sutra belongs to the gradual teaching of the five periods.
Why, then, does it directly describe the true source and wondrous enlightenment? Is it not an error to conflate the gradual with the sudden?

I reply: My ancestor’s mind roamed the Great Teaching and he attained wondrous enlightenment in the Perfect Doctrine. Every action was intended to bring about the realization of one's own mind; every word pointed toward the sudden essence as its ultimate source. As the Patriarch of the Complete and Sudden School and the Grand Master of Huayan, how could he be compared to those scholars of the Three Stages or Five Periods, or to those gradualists who seek to return to the Real through provisional means? How could they be spoken of in the same breath?
Moreover, this is the fundamental principle of a single sutra and the source from which the myriad practices arise.
The passage beginning with "Although it is true" [and so forth] constitutes the second section, which elucidates the profound through the two truths.
The sub-commentary below states: "It causes one to realize the Middle Way within the two truths, thereby giving rise to right view."

Emptiness and the provisional are both the Middle; form and emptiness have no locus of reliance, for this is the true emptiness of the primary truth (paramārtha-satya) that serves as the fundamental tenet of this sutra.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the existence and dissolution of the two truths.
The text consists of two phrases:

the first phrase signifies the simultaneous negation of both because their meanings are mutually contradictory; the second phrase signifies the simultaneous preservation of both because they function together without mutual obstruction.
Zhenguō said:
"When form and emptiness are viewed in relation to one another, there are generally three meanings:
first, the meaning of mutual opposition; second, the meaning of non-obstruction; and third, the meaning of mutual production.
He concludes by saying:
"These three non-obstructions are called 'true emptiness' (zhēn kōng) and are also termed the meaning of 'wondrous existence' (miào yǒu).

The *Jì* states: "The reason why both the ultimate and the conventional are simultaneously extinguished is as follows: the 'ultimate' (zhēn) refers to the principle of true emptiness, which constitutes the ultimate truth (zhēn dì)."
"Conventional phenomena, such as form and other dharmas, constitute the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
It is further said: "The myriad differences of dependent origination are considered conventional, while the single flavor of the absence of intrinsic nature is the ultimate (paramārtha)."

Regarding "the simultaneous vanishing of both": because the two truths are not identical and possess mutually exclusive meanings, the conventional truth is negated by the ultimate truth, causing the ultimate to vanish;
and the ultimate truth contradicts the conventional truth, causing the conventional to perish.
"When they mutually seize one another and both perish, this is called 'the simultaneous extinction of both.

It further states: "Because these dharmas of dependent origination are empty of intrinsic nature, that illusory existence is likewise rendered non-existent; therefore, all things are nothing but true emptiness."
The Sūtra says: "All phenomena are ultimately empty, without even the slightest mark.
It also says: "All phenomena are empty, like the conflagration at the end of a kalpa," and so forth.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Because form and so forth are empty, within emptiness there is no form.

Relying on the gate of illusory existence being non-existent, and relying on the gate of true emptiness being not non-empty, it is taught that this true emptiness eternally destroys illusory existence; thus, it causes conventional appearances to be eternally exhausted, thereby constituting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Furthermore, because this dharma of dependent origination possesses the characteristic of illusory existence, it causes that very emptiness to become non-empty; there is only the distinction between dependent origination and illusory existence.
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "It is not a negation of cessation followed by rebirth, because it arises through the causal conditions of continuity."

In works such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is clarified that the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is never non-existent. This is explained by relying on the gate of "emptiness within true emptiness" and the gate of "existence within illusory existence," asserting that those dependently arisen phenomena are never empty; thus, they constitute conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
In this way, the two truths only establish their respective positions through mutual negation and sublation.
The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng) states: "Because conventional truth exists, it is not empty; because ultimate truth is empty, it does not exist."
Therefore, both [extremes] are extinguished.
Regarding the phrase "the two truths eternally exist," the *Zongchi* states:
"If one says that because dependent origination is not non-existent in its nature, it is therefore 'existent through conditions,' this reveals that it does not exist inherently."

"That which does not exist by itself is without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); furthermore, that which lacks intrinsic nature reveals that it does not exist by itself; that which does not exist by itself exists through conditions.
The subsequent scripture states: "Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form."
The treatise states: "The extreme blindness and darkness of the cognitive obscuration refers to the separate apprehension of the ultimate and the conventional.
Nor can one claim that dependent origination is not admitted because of the emptiness of intrinsic nature; for without dependent origination, emptiness cannot be established."
The Treatise says: "Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are empty because they arise from conditions.
Furthermore, this is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), not a nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*).
If one were to regard something as empty only after it has arisen in dependence upon the condition of cessation, that would be the 'evil realm of emptiness' within the sphere of deluded attachment."
Therefore, the ultimate truth supersedes the conventional; yet, when the conventional is exhausted, the conventional nonetheless persists.

Furthermore, one cannot grant that because things exist through conditions, they thereby contradict or harm true emptiness; for if something were not empty, it would not be an existence through conditions, since that which exists inherently is not produced by conditions.
Therefore, when the conventional subverts the ultimate, the ultimate vanishes, yet the ultimate remains eternally present.

Furthermore, existence that is not distinct from emptiness is precisely "true emptiness," and emptiness that is not distinct from existence is precisely "illusory existence. Thus, these two are non-dual; their presence and their cessation are simultaneous.
Below the section on "Emptiness and Existence," second, the single flavor is fully manifested.
Guishan said:
"It means that the nature of the one true mind is neither empty nor material, yet it can be both empty and material, like the brightness of a mirror."

This adds the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to the two truths; it means that because there is no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), that which arises through conditions is empty and non-existent;
and because it arises through conditions, there is no intrinsic nature, meaning that existence is non-existent.
Since both emptiness and existence have perished to become the Dharma of a single flavor, it is said that it is "constantly manifest.

The sub-commentary below states: "The illusory nature of form, whether existing or non-existing, is unimpeded within true emptiness; its concealment and manifestation are sovereign as they merge into a single flavor. To be perfectly pervasive and without dependence—this is that Dharma."
"From 'Precisely because' onwards, thirdly, the Middle Way is used to reveal the Subtle.
Qingliang said:
'The intent clarifies that within this, both emptiness and existence are the Middle Way.'"

Although "illusory existence" and "true emptiness" pertain to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the various patriarchs, in their commentaries on these meanings, have mostly addressed them from the perspective of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) to describe how the established doctrines of the various schools differ and how the profundity and shallowness of the various teachings are vastly distinct.

However, since the arrival of the Xuanzang administration, profound meanings have become obscured and subtle; consequently, those who follow conventional interpretations have largely suppressed the deep sutras, treating them as expedient and shallow teachings.

Now, I shall first set forth the various schools' respective adherences to emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhāva*), presenting them clearly before me, and thereafter provide a detailed commentary on the text.
The initial statement regarding "illusory existence" is also termed "dependent existence," "sublime existence," "provisional existence," and "semblance existence.
The *Zongchi* states:
"Within this Mahāyāna, two schools vigorously debate the nature of dependently arisen phenomena."

First, the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school asserts that this dependent origination is definitively not empty, because it is produced by causes and conditions; thus, like a magical illusion, it cannot be said to be non-existent.
If one were to say that emptiness is not dependently originated, it would be like the horns of a rabbit and so forth.

Furthermore, it is said that the Three Treatises merely refute the imagined self and phenomena of the Hīnayāna and non-Buddhists, but do not refute the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of the Mahāyāna, because this is a "magical existence" (*māyopama*) and thus free from fault.
If this [position] were also refuted, it would be a nihilistic view of annihilationism, subsumed under the realm of the miserable destinies (*apāya*) and not the true Dharma.
Since this is a profound error, it is clear that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is certainly not non-existent.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and other such texts definitively teach that [phenomena] exist; therefore, one must not contradict them.
This is the explanation of the Characteristics School (Lakṣaṇavāda) within the Initial Teaching (Ādikarmika-yāna); it does not accept that this illusory existence is itself emptiness.

The proponents of the Two Emptinesses school maintain that these dependently originated phenomena are definitively empty; because they arise from conditions, they necessarily lack intrinsic nature, and like illusory phenomena, they cannot be said to exist.
If one says that [things] exist, then they do not arise from conditions; because they do not arise from conditions, they are not phenomena of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Furthermore, it is said that even the "other-dependent" (*paratantra*) established in treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is refuted by the Three Treatises (*Tri-svabhāva-śāstra*), because there is nothing produced through conditions that is not empty.
If this is not negated, it is because perception does not vanish and principle is not exhausted.
This is the explanation of the Śūnyavāda school within the Initial Teaching (Ādikarmika-yāna).

This illusory existence cannot be said to exist; if one says it exists, that is merely what is grasped by the ignorant person with cataracts, indicating that attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha) has not been exhausted.

Third is the Dharma-nature school (Faxing zong), which teaches that this illusory existence arises from conditions and lacks intrinsic nature; it is like a magically conjured person: it is not that the conjured person does not exist, yet the conjured person is not real; therefore, it is called "illusory existence."
It is also called "wondrous existence" (*miao-you*); because it takes that which is not existent as existent, it is named "wondrous existence.

Furthermore, it is said that taking form which is identical to emptiness constitutes "wondrous form"; because form manifests through the realization of the non-existence of form, it becomes "wondrous form."
It is further said that existence which is identical to emptiness is alone existence endowed with all virtues.
It is also said that the meaning of "illusory existence" is that which is neither existent nor non-existent; this is called illusory existence.
Furthermore, it is said that not falling into one-sided extremes constitutes the Middle Way within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
This refers to the Dharma-nature school’s (*dharmatā-yāna*) method of revealing the meaning of illusory existence by means of the mutual identity of emptiness and existence.

Next, regarding "true emptiness": first, the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school, based on the intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) concerning the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), states that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; this reverses the Lesser Vehicle by asserting that the six consciousnesses are empty.
The dependent and the perfected exist; they cannot be identical with emptiness. The imagined is empty, being merely non-existent, and is thus called "true emptiness.
According to the school of the two emptinesses, both mind and objects are empty, being of equal and uniform flavor.
Guifeng said:
"To take the lack of intrinsic nature in all phenomena as truth is like taking the absence of substance in illusory flowers as the great void.
He further cited the *Mahāyānadvāra-śāstra*, which says: "The profound meaning in its broadest sense is what is called emptiness."
"Provisional names and the Middle Way are discussed solely from the perspective of emptiness.
Qingliang said: "The Sanlun school states:"
To falsely claim that things exist is [to speak of] emptiness from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Based on conceptual construction (*parikalpita*), this is the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); because it is conventional, it exists.
Perfect accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna*) is the ultimate; because it is ultimate, it is empty.
"Phenomena arising from conditions certainly possess no self-nature; therefore, they are called 'empty of reality' (*śūnyatā*).
To say that they exist is itself an attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
This is the doctrine revered by masters such as Zhiguang, Zhu Tai, and Kang Lang.

Dharma Master Tai’s *Benwu Lun* (Treatise on Original Non-being) states: "It is not that existence is non-existence; it is not that non-existence is non-existence. Therefore, it is called "True Emptiness" (*zhēn kōng*).

For this reason, Master Sengzhao composed the *Buzhēnkōng Lun* (Treatise on the Non-emptiness of the True). In his *Yanyi* (Exegesis), he explains the title as follows: "The 'True Emptiness' herein is not the 'True Emptiness' that stands in contrast to 'wondrous existence. This 'True Emptiness' is the very disease to be eliminated, for [the opponent] claims that the ultimate truth (*zhēndì*) is exclusively the absence of all things, which they designate as 'True Emptiness.'"
Master Zhao [Sengzhao] negated it with "not not," stating that it does not mean unilaterally that there are no things; therefore, he said, "it is not true emptiness.
He further remarked, "This merely captures one part of the meaning of emptiness within the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises)."
Cao Tang said:
"He does not even establish the real, let alone the delusory.
He takes the ultimate truth as true emptiness."
Regarding the "true emptiness" (zhēn kōng) taught by the Three Dharma-Nature Schools, Zhenguó said:
"The emptiness that is identical to form is what is called true emptiness; it is also termed 'wondrous existence' (miào yǒu)."
It is further said: "Essentially, it is the emptiness that is identical with existence that constitutes the emptiness endowed with all virtues.
It is also said: "The emptiness that is not [merely] empty is what is endowed with all virtues.
This is precisely the true emptiness of the Middle Way as revealed by the Dharma-nature school.
Next, the commentary on the text is explained.
The text consists of four sections:
the first section contrasts and synthesizes emptiness and existence to reveal the Middle Way.

The reason why the three truths were previously explained as being perfectly interfused and of a single flavor of both emptiness and existence is precisely because illusory existence and true emptiness are non-dual, constituting the Middle Way; thus they are one.
The commentary concludes by establishing the Middle Way, stating: "Neither empty nor existent is the meaning of the Middle Way."

The *Chao* states: "However, its primary intent is that the two meanings of 'true emptiness' are collectively termed 'not empty,' and the two meanings of 'illusory existence' are collectively termed 'not existent. Because emptiness and existence are non-dual, this constitutes the Middle Way."
The two meanings of "true emptiness" (zhēnkōng) are emptiness and non-emptiness.
The two meanings of "illusion" (huàn) are existence and non-existence.
Regarding the term "true emptiness," Qingliang said:
“Emptiness by virtue of the absence of intrinsic nature is the meaning of emptiness.
Emptiness by virtue of dependent origination is the reason for emptiness; this ‘reason’ refers precisely to causes and conditions.
That is to say, how is it that through the absence of intrinsic nature the meaning of emptiness is established?”
The commentary states:
Because they arise from conditions, they lack intrinsic nature; therefore, the fact that what arises from conditions lacks intrinsic nature is the reason why it is empty.
Since phenomena arising from conditions are empty because they lack intrinsic nature, it is called "true emptiness."
Furthermore, emptiness does not depend upon the destruction of the distinct entities of phenomena before it can be realized; therefore, true emptiness has never been non-existent.
Moreover, this very existence of phenomena—being dependently originated and devoid of intrinsic nature—is precisely what is termed "true emptiness."
Therefore it is said: "By means of existence itself, one distinguishes emptiness.
Regarding what is called "illusory existence," Qingliang said:
"'Because it arises from conditions, it exists'—this is the meaning of 'existence.'"
"Because of the absence of intrinsic nature, there is the reason for the existence of this existence.
He further asked:
"On what basis can dependent origination be established as the meaning of 'existence'?"
The commentary states:
It is precisely because there is no fixed nature that things first arise from conditions as illusory existents; therefore, this lack of nature is the very reason for their existence.
Since they are existents lacking nature due to being conditioned, these existents always lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva); thus it is said that illusory existents have never not been empty.
Furthermore, this very absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) arises as existence through its entirety depending on conditions; therefore, emptiness itself clarifies existence.

However, this commentary directly clarifies that true emptiness is the true emptiness that is identical to illusory existence, and illusory existence is the illusory existence that is identical to true emptiness; thus it is said that emptiness and existence are universally integrated to manifest the Middle Way.
Below "Emptiness and Existence," second, there is a separate synthesis of emptiness and existence to reveal the Middle Way.
This means that upon each of these—the illusory existence and the true emptiness—the meaning of the Middle Way is individually revealed.
The initial statement of "existence" refers to the intrinsic nature of illusory phenomena; that is, within the state of illusory existence, it is not the case that they do not exist.

The subsequent statement of "empty-existence" means that these illusory phenomena lack inherent nature due to their dependence on conditions; this existence within emptiness is the existence of emptiness itself, and is therefore termed "empty-existence."
"Thus it does not exist" means that because its entire substance is entirely empty and non-existent, it refers to the meaning of non-existence upon illusory existence.
The non-duality of neither existing nor not existing constitutes a single illusory existence.
The *Zongchi* states: "First, the meaning of 'not being existent' refers to the fact that the entire substance is completely empty, for there is nothing whatsoever.
Second, the meaning of 'not being non-existent.'"
This means that it does not depend upon the destruction of those differentiated characteristics.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All phenomena are non-existent, yet they exist in this way. Therefore, that which is neither existent nor non-existent is called "illusory existence" (*māyopama*).

Second, "truth" (*satya*) refers here to clarity through wisdom; because noble wisdom contemplates that [the object] is examined and not false, it is called a truth.
Although ordinary beings possess suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), they do not examine them as real, and thus these cannot be called truths.
Because they are the objects thoroughly known by non-erroneous noble wisdom, they are called "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "They are called 'truths' (*satya*) for two reasons:

The *dharmatā* is the truth of reality, and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is the thorough examination of that truth.

Furthermore, Tiantai posits four types of the Four Noble Truths:
first, the truth of arising and ceasing; second, the truth of non-arising; third, the immeasurable truth; and fourth, the unconditioned truth.
When bound, there are only nature and characteristics; when characteristics unfold, there are immeasurable instances of arising and ceasing.
Within the four unconditioned states, they are likewise bound by only nature and characteristics; when characteristics unfold, there are immeasurable instances of arising and ceasing.
When nature unfolds, there is non-arising and non-conditioning. If one were to invoke the reality through its name, it would necessarily correspond to that reality.

This present sutra possesses all four [noble truths]. If categorized according to their expressed meaning (*abhidheya*), it properly corresponds to "non-action" (*anabhisaṃskāra*) while also encompassing "non-arising" (*anutpāda*). Why is this?

If one understands suffering as being without suffering and names it the Noble Truth of Suffering; if one understands origination as being without combination, cessation as being without cessation, and the path as being without a path—then by realizing that these four arise through conditions and are therefore empty, one accords with non-arising.

If one realizes that the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas) are all suchness (tathatā), there is no suffering to be abandoned; ignorance and worldly afflictions (kleśa) are themselves bodhi, so there is no origin of suffering to be severed.
Birth and death are themselves nirvana, so there is no cessation to be realized.
Extremes and deviations are all rectified within the center; there is no path to be cultivated.

Where there is no suffering and no origination, there is no mundane world; where there is no cessation and no path, there is no supramundane world. Neither grasping nor rejecting—this is the single Middle Way.
Furthermore, there is no suffering to be abandoned because it is not [inherently] existent; there is nothing to be abandoned because its essence is itself suchness (*tathatā*).
Outside of suchness, there is no suffering; what, then, is there to be abandoned?
This phrase speaks of "suchness," yet even suchness resembles emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
In this concentration, ignorance and the afflictions are all immediately bodhi; how could they be the same as the former emptiness?
There is nothing else apart from the essence of bodhi that can be severed, which differs from the emptiness of non-arising where there is nothing to be severed.
Previously, there were no flowers in the sky; how could they have been plucked?
Now, form is itself emptiness, just as waves are themselves water and cannot be removed from it—this is not the same as the extinction of form.
Birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa; it is not that their essence is empty such that there is nothing to arise or cease.

Extremes and deviance are themselves the center and correctness; it is not that there is a Middle Way apart from extremes, nor a Right Path apart from deviance, nor is it that there is no cultivation because there are no extremes and no deviance.
This is precisely the single-flavored Dharma of perfect penetration and non-obstruction in the present sutra; therefore, it is characterized by non-action (*anabhisamskāra*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The letter A is the gateway, for all phenomena are from the beginning unarisen.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains: "If a bodhisattva hears the letter A amidst all phenomena, they immediately follow its meaning; that is to say, all phenomena have the characteristic of being unarisen from the very beginning."
"A-ti" means "the beginning" in the language of Qin;
"An-ou-po-t'o" means "non-arising" in the language of Qin.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The letter *ra* awakens one to the fact that all dharmas are free from dust and defilement."
The *Śāstra* states: "If one hears the syllable *ra*, one immediately understands through its meaning that all phenomena possess the characteristic of being free from defilement (*vimala*).
This is because *raja*—in the language of Qin (Chinese)—means 'defilement' (*mala*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "'Pa' refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)."
The treatise says: "If one hears the syllable *pa*, one immediately knows that all phenomena enter the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This is because *paramārtha* is translated in the language of Qin as 'ultimate truth'."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The cultivation of the syllable 'Ca' (遮) is unobtainable.
The Treatise says: "If one hears the syllable 'Ca,' one immediately knows that all dharmas and all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are entirely non-formations."
"Because *caryā* [is translated as] 'practice' (*xing*) in the Qin language.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The letter-gateway *na*: all dharmas are devoid of name, nature, and characteristics, because they are neither obtained nor lost."
The Treatise says: "If one hears the syllable *na*, one immediately knows that all dharmas are neither gained nor lost, neither coming nor going.
*Na*—in the language of Qin (Chinese)—means 'not'."
Thus we know that even that which is not based on causes and conditions can be explained through forced interpretation.
Third, the Dedication of Merit through Celebration:
"The Prajñā is profound" is the praise.
"Difficult to encounter over many kalpas" celebrates the present encounter.
"Explaining and interpreting according to my capacity" is an expression of humility.
"Hoping to realize the True Doctrine" is a dedication toward the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
As for what is called the "True Doctrine" (Zhēnzōng), it refers to the True Doctrine of Prajñā, which is also the Great Vehicle of the Buddha-dharma.

This concludes the *Lianzhujì* (String of Pearls Commentary) on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra-śāstra*. The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra-śāstra* was composed by the Tang Dynasty Master Xuánzàng (National Teacher Xiánshǒu) at the translation hall in response to the request of Lord Zhèng.
The phrasing is concise and the purport is subtle; therefore, those who compose commentaries and extracts find this task particularly difficult to master.

Master Huìyīn, a Dharma Master of the Avataṃsaka, uniquely elucidated its profound subtleties and excelled beyond conventional discourse; he often lamented that the old chapters frequently deviated from the intent of the commentary.
One day, complying with the request of the assembly, he produced this new record titled "The String of Pearls" (*Lianzhu*).

It takes the bequeathed instructions of the patriarchs as its guiding compass and the aphorisms of the sūtras and śāstras as its model. By probing the profound and hidden depths, it is intended for future generations, so that the torches of wisdom may be passed from one to another; how great, then, must be its merit!
At the time of the mid-autumn festival, on the day after the full moon, in the year of the Yiyou cycle during the Qian Dao era of the Imperial Song dynasty,
the śramaṇa Huishi completed the *Lianzhu ji* (The String of Pearls Record),
a brief commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. Part Two, End.
